argument: Serializability requires the effect of concurrent transactions to match some serial order. Conflict graphs, locking, timestamp ordering, and optimistic control provide ways to enforce or test this abstraction.
boundary: Serializability does not itself guarantee real-time order, durability, or application invariants.
Snapshot isolation can permit write skew.
Distributed strict isolation can be expensive.
claim: Serializability requires the effect of concurrent transactions to match some serial order. Conflict graphs, locking, timestamp ordering, and optimistic control provide ways to enforce or test this abstraction.
interpretation: A transactional claim should specify isolation level and anomalies excluded. “ACID-compliant” is too coarse.

argument: Because warming tracks cumulative CO2 emissions, continued positive net emissions continue to raise temperature. Reaching approximately net-zero anthropogenic CO2 stops the dominant cumulative increase, while the eventual temperature response depends on residual non-CO2 forcing and carbon–climate feedbacks.
boundary: Net zero is a global physical condition, not automatically a fair allocation rule.
Residual emissions and removals must be durable and accurately measured.
Non-CO2 greenhouse gases require separate stabilization pathways.
claim: Because warming tracks cumulative CO2 emissions, continued positive net emissions continue to raise temperature. Reaching approximately net-zero anthropogenic CO2 stops the dominant cumulative increase, while the eventual temperature response depends on residual non-CO2 forcing and carbon–climate feedbacks.
interpretation: Net-zero claims need explicit scopes, gases, dates, boundaries, and treatment of offsets; the phrase alone is not an auditable climate Principle.
